About.title: About me
About.description: Senior Full Stack developer specialized in microservices, real-time systems and DevOps.
About.role: Senior Full Stack Developer & DevOps Architect
About.intro: Hi, I'm Tunahan İPEK. I'm a solution-oriented Senior Full Stack developer specialized in complex microservice architectures, real-time data streams and advanced DevOps processes. I have deep technical knowledge of the modern JavaScript ecosystem (Next.js, NestJS, Svelte) and container orchestration (Kubernetes). My experience spans end-to-end product development — from self-hosted infrastructure I run on my own physical servers to leading technical teams — and clean architecture, scalability and maintainable code are always my priorities.

points: Built a real-time courier & QR menu system with a cross-platform mobile app in Flutter, advanced admin panels in Next.js and a high-performance backend architecture in NestJS.
Set up Self-hosted GitLab, GitLab Runner, Harbor and MinIO on my own physical servers; managed Kubernetes (K8s) configurations via Lens and Rancher to ensure high availability.
Developed WebSocket-based bridges that stream in-game metrics to a user panel in real time, plus real-time auction apps, using Java (Netty/Protobuf).
Built custom deployment scripts with Go and set up AI-based workflow automations with n8n.
Led the Frontend, Backend, Mobile and AI (Python) teams technically; ran team management and task distribution for 7 months.
Built scalable web solutions with a Next.js and GraphQL architecture and performance-focused mobile apps with React Native.
Provided architectural support for the digital transformation projects of other companies within the holding; continued developing high-traffic personal projects outside of work hours.
Built highly secure and well-documented enterprise API services with .NET Core and NestJS.
Built SEO-friendly corporate blog sites and web applications from scratch with Next.js.
Integrated the iyzico payment infrastructure into existing projects to enable secure payment flows.
Made UX-improving interface enhancements on a Next.js-based HR platform and optimized and fixed complex bugs.
Added payment systems to Node.js and PHP-based legacy projects and resolved performance bottlenecks.
Provided debugging and architectural-improvement support to projects across different technology stacks.

experience.company: Rubiklabs Yazılım Bilişim San. ve Tic. Ltd. Şti.
points: Bizeheryer.com: Single-handedly built a comprehensive trilingual (TR, EN, NL) portal for a travel agency; set up the backend and frontend architecture and connected panel statistics with a real-time data stream.
Migrated the company's main website from Vue.js to a Next.js architecture, improving performance.
Built Svelte backoffice and TV apps for Turkcell branches, game prototypes with Three.js and custom NestJS-based packages for Proxmox.
Managed complex database schemas using RabbitMQ, Redis and GraphQL together with the Prisma, TypeORM and Knex.js ORMs.
Built desktop automation software with C# and Python (PyQt5).
Built modern, responsive websites and e-commerce platforms with HTML/CSS and React/Next.js.

Faq.title: FAQ

what.question: What is this site?
what.answer: It's my blog and portfolio where I share software, projects, and personal experiences.

tech.question: What is the site built with?
tech.answer: It's built with Next.js (App Router), TypeScript, Prisma and PostgreSQL, with Tailwind CSS and Radix UI for the interface.

addPost.question: How do I add a blog post?
addPost.answer: After registering, users with moderator or admin roles can create posts using the rich text editor on the add blog page.

publish.question: When are posts published?
publish.answer: Posts are saved as drafts and appear on the blog list after admin approval.

languages.question: Which languages is the content available in?
languages.answer: The interface is available in Turkish and English; switch anytime using the language selector in the top right.

comments.question: Can I comment on posts?
comments.answer: Yes. Once signed in, you can leave comments under posts and join the discussion.

register.question: How do I register?
register.answer: Use the register link on the login page to create an account with your email and password.

forgotPassword.question: I forgot my password, what should I do?
forgotPassword.answer: Use the “Forgot password” link on the login page to receive a reset link at your email address.

contact.question: How can I contact you?
contact.answer: Reach out via the email on the contact page or through my LinkedIn/GitHub accounts.

collaboration.question: How do I propose a collaboration or project?
collaboration.answer: I'm open to new projects. Send an email from the contact page and share your idea; I usually reply within 24 hours.

Tips.label: Did you know?
items: HTTP 418 is a real status code: 'I'm a teapot'. (A 1998 joke, still alive.)
Git's name comes from a slang word its creator Linus Torvalds used for himself.
The first computer 'bug' in 1947 was a real moth stuck in a relay.
localhost always resolves to 127.0.0.1, reserved for loopback.
JavaScript was designed in 10 days; its name borrowed Java's popularity.
git commits are addressed by the SHA-1 (now SHA-256) hash of their content.
Deleting a line of code is a contribution too: the fastest code is no code.
UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII; the first 128 chars are identical.
Cache invalidation is one of the two hard things in computer science.
Tony Hoare, who invented the null reference, calls it his 'billion-dollar mistake'.
The odds of a collision in a UUID v4 are practically zero.
Debounce waits for the last event; throttle fires on an interval.
In HTTP, GET is idempotent: repeating the same request changes nothing.
Loading an image with lazy loading speeds up the first page paint.
console.table renders arrays and objects as a readable table.
Searching an indexed column is far faster than scanning the whole table.
Semantic HTML improves accessibility and SEO with no extra effort.
git reflog can recover most 'lost' commits.
const can't be reassigned, but an object's contents can still change.
=== does no type coercion; == does, so prefer ===.
The smaller a function is, the easier it is to test.
flexbox is for one dimension, grid for two.
HTTP 301 is a permanent redirect, 302 a temporary one.
Regular expressions are greedy by default; ? makes them lazy.
z-index only works on positioned elements.
A Promise resolves or rejects exactly once.
map returns a new array, forEach does not.
Self-explanatory names beat explanatory comments.
git stash safely shelves work in progress without committing.
Browsers evaluate CSS right-to-left, so selectors matter.
JSON has no comments by design; it's a deliberate choice.
API versioning makes managing breaking changes much easier.
0, '', null, undefined and NaN are 'falsy' in JavaScript.
Use a Set for unique fast lookups, a Map for key-value pairs.
Mobile-first design keeps your media queries simpler.
try/finally runs cleanup code whether or not an error is thrown.
An accessible button should always be a real <button>, not a div.
The TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) sets up a connection before data flows.
HTTPS uses TLS; the handshake negotiates keys before any encrypted data is sent.
A CDN serves assets from edge locations near the user to cut latency.
DNS resolution is cached at multiple layers; TTL controls for how long.
Idempotent HTTP methods: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD; POST is not.
CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server; the server only sends headers.
A JWT has three parts: header, payload, signature — the payload is not encrypted.
Hash passwords with bcrypt/argon2 and a salt; never store them in plain text.
SQL injection is prevented with parameterized queries, not string concatenation.
An index speeds up reads but slows down writes and uses extra storage.
Database normalization reduces redundancy; denormalization can speed up reads.
ACID: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees of transactions.
The CAP theorem: under a partition, you choose between consistency and availability.
Connection pooling reuses DB connections instead of opening one per request.
A foreign key enforces referential integrity between tables.
Big-O describes how an algorithm scales, not its exact runtime.
Binary search runs in O(log n) but requires sorted data.
A hash map offers average O(1) lookups; the worst case is O(n) on collisions.
Recursion without a base case leads to a stack overflow.
Memoization trades memory for speed by caching results.
Immutability makes state changes predictable and easier to debug.
Pure functions have no side effects and return the same output for the same input.
The event loop lets single-threaded JS handle async work without blocking.
Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (setTimeout) in the event loop.
Debounce delays execution until activity stops; throttle limits frequency.
The DOM is a tree; reflow recalculates layout, repaint redraws pixels.
CSS specificity: inline > id > class > element; avoid !important.
The box model: content, padding, border, margin — box-sizing changes how width is computed.
Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH signals the impact of a change.
Git is distributed; every clone is a full repository with its history.
A merge keeps history as-is; a rebase rewrites it for a linear log.
.gitignore prevents files from being tracked, not from being deleted.
Code review catches bugs early and spreads knowledge across the team.
Unit tests check a single unit; integration tests check how parts work together.
Test coverage shows executed lines, not whether the behavior is correct.
CI runs tests automatically on every push to catch regressions early.
Feature flags let you ship code dark and enable it without redeploying.
Blue-green deployment swaps traffic between two identical environments.
Containers share the host kernel; VMs include a full guest OS.
Stateless services scale horizontally more easily than stateful ones.
A load balancer distributes requests across multiple servers.
Rate limiting protects an API from abuse and overload.
Caching layers — browser, CDN, application, database — each cut latency.
A 429 status means too many requests; respect the Retry-After header.
ETags let the browser revalidate a cached resource without re-downloading it.
Lazy loading defers offscreen content to speed up the initial render.
Tree shaking removes unused code from the final bundle.
Minification and gzip/brotli compression shrink payloads over the wire.
The critical rendering path determines how fast a page becomes visible.
Web accessibility (a11y) follows WCAG; color contrast and keyboard nav matter.
ARIA enhances accessibility, but native HTML elements should be preferred first.
UTF-8 encodes characters in 1–4 bytes and dominates the modern web.
Endianness is the byte order of multi-byte values in memory.
A race condition occurs when output depends on uncontrolled timing.
A deadlock happens when processes wait on each other forever.
Garbage collection frees unreferenced memory automatically.
A memory leak is memory that is never released though no longer needed.
The principle of least privilege grants only the access that is needed.
Defense in depth layers multiple security controls on top of each other.
Never trust client input; always validate and sanitize on the server.
HTTPS everywhere prevents man-in-the-middle attacks on plain HTTP.
Secrets belong in environment variables or a vault, never in source code.
A webhook pushes events to you; polling repeatedly asks for updates.
GraphQL lets clients request exactly the fields they need.
REST is stateless; each request carries all the context it needs.
git status shows what is staged, unstaged, and untracked.
git add -p stages changes hunk by hunk for cleaner commits.
git commit --amend edits the last commit — avoid it after pushing.
git log --oneline --graph shows a compact visual history.
git diff --staged shows what will go into the next commit.
git restore --staged <file> unstages a file without losing changes.
git switch -c <branch> creates and switches to a new branch.
git cherry-pick applies a single commit from another branch.
git rebase -i lets you squash, reorder, and edit commits.
git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes a commit but keeps the changes staged.
git reset --hard discards changes permanently — use with care.
git revert creates a new commit that safely undoes a previous one.
git fetch downloads changes without merging; git pull does both.
git pull --rebase keeps history linear instead of adding a merge commit.
git blame <file> shows who last changed each line.
git bisect binary-searches commits to find the one that broke things.
git tag marks a commit, often used for releases.
git clean -fd removes untracked files and directories.
A detached HEAD means you are on a commit, not a branch.
Write commit messages in the imperative: 'Add feature', not 'Added feature'.
git remote -v lists the remote repositories and their URLs.
git merge --no-ff always creates a merge commit, preserving branch history.

intro.title: Overview
intro.body: This policy explains how personal data is processed on blog.tunahanipek.com and related services. We use your data only to provide the service, maintain security, and respond to your requests. We do not sell your data to third parties.

data.title: Data we collect
data.body: When you register, we may process email, name, profile details, and session records. Messages sent via the contact form (name, email, and content) are kept only to respond to you. Limited technical logs (IP, browser type) may be retained for security and performance.

cookies.title: Cookies and analytics
cookies.body: Essential cookies are required for the site to function. Preference and analytics cookies are enabled only after you accept them in the cookie banner. You can withdraw consent at any time via browser settings or the banner.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.body: You may request access, correction, deletion, or object to processing under applicable privacy laws. We review and respond to requests within a reasonable timeframe.

contact.title: Contact the data controller
contact.body: For any privacy-related request, email hello@tunahanipek.com. We may ask for additional information to verify your identity solely to handle your request securely.

content.title: Content and intellectual property

account.title: Account and security
account.body: You are responsible for keeping your credentials confidential. Accounts may be suspended or permanently closed if spam, abuse, or security violations are detected.

liability.title: Limitation of liability
liability.body: The site is provided "as is." We aim to resolve outages and maintenance issues promptly but are not liable for indirect or unforeseeable damages.

changes.title: Updates

mottos: while (sleep < enough) { coffee++; }
Life is a try; the rest is catch (everything) { }
If it works in production — don't touch it. (Seriously.)
I live inside an array: while (true)
When a bug becomes a feature, I call it feature.
Pray before git push. Then push anyway.
Code runs. Why? Unknown. Good enough.
Every commit tells a story; every deployment teaches a lesson.
Spouse: 'What did you do today?' Me: 'Deleted a comma.' (4 hrs.)
I never commit without Stack Overflow. (Lie. I always do.)
undefined is not a function — you again, JavaScript?
30 min debugging, 8 sec typo. Classic final boss.
Fixed merge conflict. Soul still in CONFLICT state.
Hotfix = hot coffee + panic + git push --force (kidding, don't.)
Said I'd refactor. Rewrote all the CSS. (Again.)
End of day: not shutdown, sleep(28800)
Two kinds of people: array[0] vs array[1] fans.
Async life: callback never arrived. Still waiting.
Boolean mode: true = code, false = thinking about code.
SELECT * FROM life — too many rows, need an index.
Doctor: stress? Me: no, npm install is stuck.
Wrote 'LGTM' in code review. No idea what it means. Sounds confident.
Worked on my machine. Sure. Everything worked on my machine.
Think twice before rm -rf. (Once isn't enough either.)
Forgot a semicolon. JavaScript forgave me. I didn't.
it works — just don't ask me how.
Best docs ever: 'read the code'. Thanks, super helpful.
Cleared the cache. Bug gone. Reason? Unknown, don't ask.
Estimate: 2 hours. Reality: 2 days. Classic.
Variable named data. What's inside? Data. Of course.
console.log('did it reach here') — modern debugging.
If meetings turned into code, we'd never write a line.
New framework dropped. I just learned the old one.
Client: 'Tiny change.' Me: starting to sweat.
0.1 + 0.2 equals 0.30000000000004 — just accept it.
Tabs or spaces? That's how we stopped being friends.
Out of coffee = out of builds. Both need a restart.
Comment: 'No idea why this works, but don't delete it.'
Deploy on Friday at 5pm. Brave or dumb? Yes.
Wrote a regex. Now I have two problems.
Deleted the code, fixed the bug. Cleanest refactor ever.
Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V — senior engineer shortcuts.
Didn't write tests because I trust myself. Mistake.
I don't code without dark mode. Light is a bug to me.
Boss: 'Simple thing.' Repo: 14 microservices down.
npm audit: 4096 vulnerabilities. Ignoring, politely.
Pair programming: one writes, one opens YouTube.
Code fails: panic. Code works: bigger panic.
Hit an infinite loop. Made tea. It's still spinning.
Opened old code. Did I write this? God help me.
404: motivation not found. But the deadline is here.
